stem:
Given this markup, what are `list.children.length` and `list.childNodes.length`? ```html
  • A
  • B
```

options.text: 2 and 5
options.why: `children` holds only element nodes; `childNodes` also holds the three whitespace text nodes around the items.

options.text: 2 and 2, because whitespace between tags is ignored by the parser
options.why: The HTML parser keeps whitespace between tags as text nodes inside the list.

options.text: 5 and 2, because `children` counts every kind of node
options.why: It is the other way round: `childNodes` includes text and comment nodes, `children` only elements.

options.text: 2 and 4, one text node before each item
options.why: There is also a trailing text node (the newline before ``), giving 3 text nodes.

explanation: The text nodes are the newline and indentation before the first item, between the items, and before the closing tag. `children` returns an HTMLCollection of elements only, which is usually what you want; `childNodes` returns a NodeList of every node type.

stem: A comment widget shows the user's name with `el.innerHTML = 'Posted by ' + name;`. A user registers with the name ``. What is the safest fix?

options.text: Keep innerHTML but wrap the name in quotes so the browser treats the markup inside as an attribute value
options.why: Quotes in a string concatenation do not change how innerHTML parses the markup.

options.text: Set `el.textContent` instead, so the name is inserted as text
options.why: textContent never parses HTML, so the tags are shown literally and nothing runs.

options.text: Strip every `<script>` tag from the name before assigning it to innerHTML
options.why: The payload has no script tag; event-handler attributes like onerror run without one.

options.text: Use `innerText` with innerHTML as a fallback for older browsers that lack it
options.why: Falling back to innerHTML reintroduces the vulnerability.

explanation: Assigning untrusted strings to innerHTML is the classic DOM-based XSS sink. textContent (or creating text nodes) treats the value as plain text. If you genuinely need HTML from users, sanitise it with a vetted library such as DOMPurify or the Sanitizer API.
reference: OWASP: DOM-based XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: Inside an event listener, `event.target` always refers to the element the listener was attached to.

options.text: True
options.why: That describes `event.currentTarget`, not `event.target`.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `event.target` is where the event started, which can be a descendant of the listening element.

explanation: With delegation the difference matters: a listener on a `<ul>` sees `currentTarget` as the list, while `target` is whichever `<li>`, `<span>` or text-wrapping element the user actually clicked.

stem: A page includes `<script defer src="a.js"></script>` followed by `<script defer src="b.js"></script>`. `b.js` is much smaller and finishes downloading first. When do the scripts run?

options.text: `b.js` first, as soon as it finishes downloading, and then `a.js`
options.why: That is how `async` scripts behave; deferred scripts keep document order.

options.text: Each one runs the moment it downloads, pausing the HTML parser while it runs
options.why: Deferred scripts never interrupt parsing; they wait until parsing is finished.

options.text: `a.js` then `b.js`, after the HTML is parsed and before `DOMContentLoaded`
options.why: Deferred scripts run in document order once parsing completes.

options.text: After the `load` event, once all images and stylesheets have also finished loading
options.why: Deferred scripts run before DOMContentLoaded, well before load.

explanation: `defer` downloads in parallel with parsing and executes in document order after parsing ends, just before DOMContentLoaded fires. `async` also downloads in parallel but runs each script as soon as it arrives, in any order, which suits independent scripts like analytics.
reference: HTML Standard: script element (defer and async)

stem: A form handler validates input with JavaScript. Without any extra code, the browser submits the form and navigates away even when validation fails. Which call inside the `submit` listener stops that?

options.text: `event.stopPropagation()`, which stops the submission from reaching the browser
options.why: stopPropagation only stops other listeners on ancestors; the default action still happens.

options.text: `event.preventDefault()`
options.why: It cancels the default action of the event, which for submit is sending the form.

options.text: `return false` from a listener that was added with `addEventListener`
options.why: Return values from addEventListener listeners are ignored; that trick only works for `onsubmit` properties.

options.text: `form.reset()`, so that there is nothing left to submit
options.why: Resetting clears the fields but the submission still goes ahead.

explanation: Default actions (following a link, submitting a form, toggling a checkbox) are separate from propagation. `preventDefault()` cancels the default action; `stopPropagation()` only stops the event travelling to other elements. The `return false` shortcut works for inline `on…` handler properties, not addEventListener.

stem: Match each browser storage mechanism with the description that fits it.

options.text: localStorage
options.why: Persistent, synchronous, per origin.

options.text: sessionStorage
options.why: Scoped to one tab and cleared when it closes.

options.text: Cookies
options.why: Small and sent to the server with requests.

options.text: IndexedDB
options.why: Asynchronous structured storage for large data.

prompts.text: Synchronous string key-value store, shared by every tab of the origin and kept after the browser restarts
String key-value store for a single tab, cleared when that tab is closed
A few kilobytes each, attached automatically to matching HTTP requests
Asynchronous, transactional store for structured objects and blobs, suitable for hundreds of megabytes

explanation: Choose by access pattern: cookies when the server needs the value on every request, Web Storage for small client-only strings, and IndexedDB for large or structured data, offline caches and anything you don't want to block the main thread for.

stem: A session cookie is set with `Set-Cookie: sid=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure`. What does the `HttpOnly` flag do?

options.text: The cookie is only sent over plain HTTP, never over HTTPS
options.why: The name is misleading; Secure controls HTTPS, and HttpOnly is about script access.

options.text: Scripts cannot read it through `document.cookie`
options.why: The browser still sends it with requests, but page JavaScript cannot see it.

options.text: The cookie is sent only on same-site requests, never on cross-site ones
options.why: That is what the SameSite attribute controls.

options.text: The cookie is deleted automatically when the user closes the tab
options.why: Lifetime depends on Expires/Max-Age; no attribute means a session cookie.

explanation: HttpOnly limits the damage of XSS: injected script can't read the session ID and send it elsewhere, although it can still make requests from the page. Secure means the cookie is only sent over HTTPS, and SameSite controls cross-site sending.

stem: A page is served from `https://app.example.com/page`. Which of these URLs has the same origin?

options.text: `http://app.example.com/page`, since only the scheme differs
options.why: The scheme is part of the origin, so http and https are different origins.

options.text: `https://api.example.com/page`, since both share the example.com domain
options.why: Origins compare the full host; subdomains are different origins.

options.text: `https://app.example.com:443/other`
options.why: Same scheme and host, and 443 is the default HTTPS port; the path is not part of the origin.

options.text: `https://app.example.com:8443/page`, since the host name is identical
options.why: An explicit different port makes it a different origin.

explanation: An origin is the triple (scheme, host, port). The path never matters, and an explicit default port (443 for https, 80 for http) is the same as leaving it out. Same-site is a looser idea: `app.example.com` and `api.example.com` are cross-origin but same-site.

stem: Which `Element` method returns the element itself or its nearest ancestor that matches a CSS selector, or `null` if none does? Type the method name.
explanation: `event.target.closest('li')` is the standard way to find the item that was clicked in a delegated listener, even when the click landed on a nested `` or `` inside it.

stem: Which two of these events do NOT bubble? (Choose two.)

options.text: `focus`
options.why: focus does not bubble; its bubbling counterpart is focusin.

options.text: `mouseenter`
options.why: mouseenter fires on each element entered and does not bubble, unlike mouseover.

options.text: `click`
options.why: click bubbles all the way up to the document and window.

options.text: `focusin`
options.why: focusin exists precisely because it bubbles, unlike focus.

options.text: `input`
options.why: input bubbles, so one listener on a form can watch all its fields.

options.text: `keydown`
options.why: keydown bubbles from the focused element.

explanation: focus/blur, mouseenter/mouseleave, load and scroll on elements are the common non-bubbling events. You can still catch them on an ancestor with a capture-phase listener, or use the bubbling twins focusin/focusout and mouseover/mouseout.

stem: A team moves a heavy image-processing loop into a Web Worker. Inside the worker, the code calls `document.querySelector('#preview')`. What happens?

options.text: It works but is slow, because each DOM call is forwarded to the main thread
options.why: There is no DOM proxy; workers simply have no document.

options.text: It returns the element, because a worker shares the page's global scope
options.why: Workers have their own global scope (DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope), separate from window.

options.text: It throws, because workers have no `document` or DOM access
options.why: The worker must post results back and let the main thread update the DOM.

options.text: It returns `null` until the main thread grants DOM access through postMessage
options.why: No such permission exists; DOM access is never available in a worker.

explanation: Workers run on another thread with no DOM, window or document. They communicate with the page using `postMessage` and can use fetch, IndexedDB, timers and OffscreenCanvas. The pattern is: compute in the worker, send the result, render on the main thread.

options.text: All four elements lose the class, because the loop visits each index once
options.why: The collection shrinks as you go, so indexes shift under the loop.

options.text: Only the first and third elements lose the class
options.why: Each removal drops an element from the live collection, so every other one is skipped.

options.text: Only the first element loses the class, and then the loop ends
options.why: The loop continues while i is below the shrinking length, which takes two iterations.

options.text: It throws, because a collection cannot change while it is being looped over
options.why: Live collections update silently; there is no concurrent-modification error.

explanation: `getElementsByClassName` returns a live HTMLCollection. i=0 removes item 1, leaving [2,3,4] with length 3. i=1 now points at item 3 and removes it, leaving [2,4] with length 2. i=2 ends the loop. Use `querySelectorAll` (a static NodeList), loop backwards, or copy with `Array.from` first.

stem: The page contains `<input id="name" value="hello">`. The user changes the text to `world`. What do `input.getAttribute('value')` and `input.value` return?

options.text: `'world'` and `'world'`, since the attribute tracks what the user typed
options.why: Typing changes the property only; the attribute keeps its original markup value.

options.text: `'hello'` and `'world'`
options.why: The attribute is the initial value (also exposed as defaultValue); the property is the current value.

options.text: `'world'` and `'hello'`, because the property keeps the initial markup value
options.why: It is the reverse: the property is live and the attribute is the default.

options.text: `null` and `'world'`, because the attribute is cleared once the user edits
options.why: The attribute stays in the DOM exactly as written.

explanation: For form controls, attributes describe the initial state and properties the current state. `value` and `checked` properties are live, while the `value` and `checked` attributes map to `defaultValue` and `defaultChecked`. That is why `form.reset()` can restore the original values.

stem: A `<button>` sits inside a `<div>`. Listeners are registered on the document in the capture phase, on the div in the capture phase, on the button, on the div in the bubble phase, and on the document in the bubble phase. Put them in the order they run when the button is clicked.

options.text: Document capture-phase listener
options.why: Capture starts at the top.

options.text: Div capture-phase listener
options.why: Capture moves down towards the target.

options.text: Button listener
options.why: At the target.

options.text: Div bubble-phase listener
options.why: Bubbling moves back up.

options.text: Document bubble-phase listener
options.why: Bubbling ends at the top.

explanation: Dispatch has three phases: capture (window down to the target's parent), target, and bubble (the target's parent back up to window). Listeners added with `{ capture: true }` run on the way down; ordinary listeners run on the way up.

options.text: `A` only, because stopPropagation stops all remaining listeners
options.why: That is stopImmediatePropagation; stopPropagation still lets the button's other listeners run.
Both listeners on the button run; the event just never reaches the parent.

options.text: `A`, `B`, `P`, because the button's second listener re-enables propagation
options.why: Listeners cannot restart propagation once it has been stopped.

options.text: `A`, `P`, because only the listener that called the method is skipped afterwards
options.why: The parent is exactly the one that gets skipped.

explanation: `stopPropagation()` prevents the event moving to other elements but lets remaining listeners on the current element finish. `stopImmediatePropagation()` also skips the remaining listeners on the current element. Neither cancels the default action.

stem: A product page has a large hero image and many thumbnails. Analytics code must run as soon as the DOM can be queried, and a carousel needs the images' final sizes. Which events should each use?

options.text: Both should use `load`, because the DOM is not ready to query until then
options.why: Waiting for every image delays the analytics for no reason.

options.text: Analytics on `DOMContentLoaded`, the carousel on `load` (or on each image's own load)
options.why: DOMContentLoaded fires once the HTML is parsed; load waits for images too.

options.text: Analytics on `load`, the carousel on `DOMContentLoaded`, so the carousel starts sooner
options.why: DOMContentLoaded does not wait for images, so sizes may still be unknown.

options.text: Both should use `DOMContentLoaded`, which already waits for images in the viewport
options.why: DOMContentLoaded never waits for images, in or out of the viewport.

explanation: DOMContentLoaded fires after the document is parsed and deferred scripts have run; it doesn't wait for images, iframes or (usually) stylesheets. load on window waits for all subresources. For a single image, listen for its own load event or use `img.decode()`.

stem: Which two statements about `fetch` are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: A request that returns HTTP 404 resolves, with `response.ok === false`
options.why: fetch only rejects on network-level failures; HTTP errors are normal responses.

options.text: Calling `response.json()` a second time on the same response rejects with a TypeError
options.why: A body is a stream that can be consumed once; clone the response to read it twice.

options.text: A request that returns HTTP 500 rejects, so a `.catch` handler sees it
options.why: A 500 response resolves like any other response.

options.text: By default, cookies are sent with cross-origin requests too
options.why: The default credentials mode is same-origin; cross-origin needs credentials: include.

options.text: A request with no timeout set is aborted by the browser after 30 seconds
options.why: fetch has no built-in timeout; use AbortSignal.timeout() or an AbortController.

explanation: Typical wrapper: `const r = await fetch(url); if (!r.ok) throw new Error(r.status); return r.json();`. Remember the body can be read once (`r.clone()` if you need it twice), credentials default to same-origin, and there is no default timeout.

stem: A scroll-linked effect adds `window.addEventListener('wheel', onWheel, { passive: true })`. Inside `onWheel`, the code calls `event.preventDefault()` to stop the page scrolling. What happens?

options.text: Scrolling stops, because preventDefault always cancels the default action
options.why: Passive listeners promise not to cancel, so the browser ignores the call.

options.text: The page still scrolls; the browser ignores the call and logs a console warning
options.why: A passive listener cannot cancel the event.

options.text: The browser throws, because preventDefault is not allowed inside passive listeners
options.why: Nothing is thrown; the call is simply ignored.

options.text: Scrolling stops, but only for the first wheel event after the page loads
options.why: The flag applies to every event this listener receives.

explanation: `passive: true` tells the browser it can scroll immediately without waiting for your listener, which keeps scrolling smooth. In return, preventDefault is ignored. Chrome and Firefox also make wheel and touch listeners on window, document and body passive by default, so code that must block scrolling needs `{ passive: false }` explicitly.

stem: Calling `localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark')` fires a `storage` event in the same tab that made the change.

options.text: True
options.why: The storage event fires in other documents of the same origin, not in the one that wrote.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: only other tabs and windows of the same origin receive the storage event.

explanation: The storage event is a cross-tab sync signal: another tab can listen for it and apply the new theme. The tab that wrote the value already knows about the change, so it gets no event. For richer messaging, use BroadcastChannel.

stem: `bank.example` sets its session cookie with `SameSite=Lax`. A user logged in to the bank visits `evil.example`. Which request from that page sends the session cookie to the bank?

options.text: An auto-submitting hidden `<form method="POST">` that targets the bank's transfer endpoint
options.why: Lax withholds cookies on cross-site POSTs, which blocks this classic CSRF.

options.text: A `fetch()` to the bank's API with `credentials: 'include'` from the evil page's script
options.why: Lax cookies are not sent on cross-site subresource or fetch requests.

options.text: The user clicking an ordinary link to `https://bank.example/account`
options.why: Top-level GET navigations are allowed to carry Lax cookies.

options.text: An `` tag whose src points at a bank URL that has side effects
options.why: Images are cross-site subresource requests, so Lax cookies are withheld.

explanation: SameSite=Lax sends the cookie on same-site requests and on cross-site top-level navigations using safe methods like GET. It withholds it from cross-site POSTs, iframes, images and fetches. That is why state-changing actions must never use GET. Strict also withholds cookies on cross-site link clicks.

stem: Which `addEventListener` option takes an `AbortSignal`, so that one `controller.abort()` call removes every listener that was registered with it? Type the option name.
explanation: `el.addEventListener('click', h, { signal: controller.signal })`. When the component unmounts, `controller.abort()` removes all of those listeners at once, with no need to keep references to each handler for removeEventListener.

options.text: `3`, because appending a fragment copies its children into the list
options.why: The children are moved, not copied.
Inserting a fragment moves its children into the target, leaving it empty.

options.text: `1`, because the fragment itself becomes the list's only child
options.why: The fragment node is never inserted; only its children are.

options.text: It throws, because a fragment cannot be appended to an element that is already in the page
options.why: Appending a fragment to a live element is the normal use.

explanation: A DocumentFragment is a lightweight container that is not in the page. Building nodes there and inserting it once means one insertion into the live document instead of many. After insertion the fragment is empty and can be reused. `<template>` content is a DocumentFragment too.

stem: Which statement about `<script type="module" src="app.js">` is true?

options.text: It blocks the HTML parser until it has downloaded and run, like a classic script
options.why: Module scripts never block the parser.

options.text: It is deferred by default and runs in strict mode
options.why: It runs after parsing in document order, and module code is always strict.

options.text: It can load a module from another origin without that server sending CORS headers
options.why: Cross-origin module scripts are fetched in CORS mode and need the right headers.

options.text: Its top-level `const` and `let` declarations become properties of `window`
options.why: Each module has its own scope; top-level bindings are not globals.

explanation: Module scripts behave like `defer` unless you add `async`. They are always strict, have their own top-level scope, run once even if included twice, and are fetched with CORS. `import.meta` and top-level await are only available inside modules.

options.text: String concatenation in the loop is slow; use template literals instead
options.why: String building is trivial next to layout work.

options.text: Each style write repaints the page at once; wrap the loop in a setTimeout callback
options.why: Painting happens later in the frame; delaying the loop doesn't remove the per-iteration layouts.

options.text: Each `offsetWidth` read after a write forces a fresh layout; read every width first, then write
options.why: Batching all reads before all writes needs only one layout.

options.text: Inline styles are slow; set the widths through a CSS class instead
options.why: Using a class does not stop the read-after-write layouts when widths differ per box.

explanation: This is layout thrashing (forced synchronous layout). After a style write, the layout is dirty, so the next `offsetWidth` read makes the browser recalculate layout immediately, 500 times. First collect all widths (`const w = boxes.map(b => b.offsetWidth)`), then apply all writes. Libraries like fastdom formalise this read/write batching.
reference: web.dev: Avoid large, complex layouts and layout thrashing

stem: A script has just changed some styles. Which three of these operations force the browser to run layout synchronously? (Choose three.)

options.text: Reading `el.offsetHeight`
options.why: Geometry properties need an up-to-date layout to return a correct value.

options.text: Calling `el.getBoundingClientRect()`
options.why: It returns layout boxes, so pending layout must be done first.

options.text: Reading `el.scrollTop`
options.why: Scroll positions depend on layout, so reading them flushes it.

options.text: Calling `el.classList.add('open')`
options.why: Changing classes only marks styles dirty; the work is deferred until needed.

options.text: Setting `el.style.transform = 'translateX(10px)'`
options.why: Writes are batched; it is reading geometry afterwards that forces work.

options.text: Reading `el.dataset.id`
options.why: Data attributes are plain strings with no dependence on layout.

explanation: Writes (class changes, style assignments) are cheap because the browser defers style and layout to the next frame. Reads of geometry (offset*, client*, scroll*, getBoundingClientRect, getComputedStyle values that depend on layout, focus with scroll, innerText) force any pending work to happen right now.

stem: A drawer animates in by changing `left` from `-300px` to `0` on every frame, and it stutters on low-end phones. Which change helps most?

options.text: Animate `margin-left` instead of `left`, since margins are calculated more cheaply
options.why: margin-left is also a layout property, so every frame still reflows.

options.text: Animate `transform: translateX()` instead, so the move happens on the compositor
options.why: Transform and opacity changes skip layout and paint and can run off the main thread.

options.text: Use setInterval at 16 ms instead of requestAnimationFrame for steadier timing
options.why: setInterval is not synced with frames and tends to make jank worse.

options.text: Set `display: none` on the drawer between frames to reset its layout
options.why: That forces even more layout and paint work.

explanation: The pipeline is style → layout → paint → composite. Changing `left`, `width` or `top` reruns layout and paint every frame. `transform` and `opacity` on a promoted layer only need compositing, which the GPU can do even while the main thread is busy. Use `will-change: transform` sparingly to promote the layer ahead of time.

stem: A page on `https://app.example` calls an API on `https://api.example`. Which of these requests makes the browser send a CORS preflight (`OPTIONS`) first?

options.text: `fetch(url)`, a plain GET with no custom headers
options.why: A simple GET needs no preflight; the server's CORS headers decide if the page can read the response.

options.text: A POST whose body is `URLSearchParams`, sent as `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`
options.why: That content type is a CORS-safelisted one, so the request is simple.

options.text: A POST with header `Content-Type: application/json`
options.why: application/json is not a safelisted content type, so a preflight is required.

options.text: A POST whose body is a plain string sent as `text/plain`
options.why: text/plain is safelisted too, so no preflight is sent.

explanation: Simple requests use GET, HEAD or POST with only safelisted headers, and a Content-Type of `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data` or `text/plain`. Anything else (JSON bodies, an `Authorization` header, PUT or DELETE) gets a preflight. Those three content types match what HTML forms could always send cross-origin.

stem: The page calls `fetch('https://api.example/me', { credentials: 'include' })`. The API responds with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. What happens?

options.text: It works: the wildcard allows every origin, including requests that carry credentials
options.why: The wildcard is not allowed together with credentials.

options.text: The browser blocks the page from reading the response; the server must echo the exact origin
options.why: Credentialed requests need a specific allowed origin, not *.

options.text: The browser quietly drops the cookies and then returns the response to the page
options.why: The browser doesn't retry without credentials; the response is just blocked.

options.text: The request is never sent, because the browser knows the response will be rejected
options.why: The browser can only check the headers after the response arrives.

explanation: For credentialed CORS the response must name the origin (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example`), send `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, and should add `Vary: Origin` so caches don't serve one origin's response to another. Echoing any Origin without an allowlist is a serious security hole.
reference: Fetch Standard: CORS protocol and credentials

stem: Match each requirement with the observer API built for it.

options.text: IntersectionObserver
options.why: Visibility relative to the viewport or a container.

options.text: ResizeObserver
options.why: Changes to an element's own size.

options.text: MutationObserver
options.why: Changes to the DOM tree or attributes.

options.text: PerformanceObserver
options.why: Performance timeline entries.

prompts.text: Start loading images when they come within 200px of the viewport
Re-layout a chart whenever its container is resized, even if the window size stays the same
Notice when a third-party widget inserts new nodes into a container
Report long tasks and Largest Contentful Paint entries to analytics

explanation: Observers replace polling and expensive event handlers. They deliver batched, asynchronous callbacks without forcing layout on every scroll or change. IntersectionObserver supports rootMargin for 'near the viewport' checks, and ResizeObserver reacts to element size rather than window size.
reference: MDN: Intersection Observer API; Resize Observer API

options.text: Clicks on the span bubble to the list without passing the li; use a capture listener instead
options.why: The event does pass through the li, but target stays the span either way.

options.text: A click on the span makes the span `e.target`; use `e.target.closest('li')` and check that the list contains it
options.why: closest walks up from the real target to the item.

options.text: matches() only works on elements that have an id; give every li its own id
options.why: matches works with any selector on any element.

options.text: dataset is not available inside event handlers; read the attribute with getAttribute instead
options.why: dataset works in handlers; the problem is which element is the target.

explanation: `event.target` is the deepest element clicked, here the span. `const li = e.target.closest('li'); if (li && list.contains(li)) select(li.dataset.id);` handles any nested markup. The contains check stops matches from an `<li>` outside the list if the selector is broad.

options.text: `before`, `after`, `handler false`, because the click event is queued as a task
options.why: click() dispatches synchronously, not through the task queue.

options.text: `before`, `handler false`, `after`
options.why: The handler runs synchronously inside click(), and script-created events are untrusted.

options.text: `before`, `handler true`, `after`, because click() simulates a real mouse click
options.why: Only events from real user input are trusted.

options.text: `before`, `after`, because click() fires no listeners added with addEventListener
options.why: click() does run every registered click listener.

explanation: `element.click()` and `dispatchEvent()` run listeners synchronously, before the next line executes, unlike user events that arrive as tasks. Such events have `isTrusted === false`, which is why browsers won't let them do some user-activation things, such as opening some popups or entering fullscreen.

stem: A page has deferred scripts and several large images. Put these steps of the page load in order.

options.text: `document.readyState` becomes `interactive`
options.why: Parsing is finished.

options.text: The deferred scripts run
options.why: They run after parsing.

options.text: `DOMContentLoaded` fires
options.why: It fires after the deferred scripts.

options.text: `document.readyState` becomes `complete`
options.why: All subresources have loaded.

options.text: The window `load` event fires
options.why: It fires last.

explanation: When parsing ends, the HTML spec sets readyState to interactive, then runs the deferred scripts, then fires DOMContentLoaded. Once images and other subresources finish, readyState becomes complete and the load event fires on window. A deferred script that checks `document.readyState` therefore sees 'interactive'.

stem: Several `<script async>` tags always run in the order they appear in the document.

options.text: True
options.why: Async scripts run as soon as each finishes downloading, so their order is not guaranteed.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: async scripts run in whatever order they arrive; use defer or modules when order matters.

explanation: async suits independent scripts such as analytics, which must not depend on each other or on DOMContentLoaded. If script B needs script A, use defer for both (document order) or import A from B as an ES module.

stem: A team says: "Our API sends strict CORS headers that only allow our own origin, so cross-site request forgery is impossible." Why is that wrong for a cookie-authenticated `POST /transfer` that accepts form-encoded bodies?

options.text: CORS headers are ignored for every POST request, so they never protect POST endpoints at all
options.why: CORS still governs what pages can read; it is just not a CSRF defence.

options.text: A cross-site form POST is a simple request: it is sent with cookies, and CORS only stops the attacker reading the response
options.why: The state change happens on the server even though the response is blocked.

options.text: Attackers can turn off CORS in their own browser and then send the request with the user's cookies
options.why: An attacker's own browser doesn't hold the victim's cookies.

options.text: CORS only applies to requests sent with fetch, so a request from an XMLHttpRequest skips every CORS check
options.why: XMLHttpRequest follows the same CORS rules as fetch.

explanation: CORS is a read-protection mechanism enforced by the browser, not an access control on the server. Simple requests (form-encoded POSTs) are sent without a preflight. Defend with SameSite cookies plus anti-CSRF tokens, by requiring a non-simple header or a JSON content type (which forces a preflight), or by checking the Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site headers.
reference: OWASP: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: A page embeds a payment iframe from `https://pay.example` and listens for its messages with `window.addEventListener('message', onMessage)`. Which two practices are required for safety? (Choose two.)

options.text: Check `event.origin === 'https://pay.example'` exactly before acting on the message
options.why: Any window can post to yours, so the sender must be verified.

options.text: Treat `event.data` as untrusted: validate its shape and never pass it to innerHTML or eval
options.why: Even a trusted origin can be compromised or send unexpected data.

options.text: Check that `event.origin.includes('pay.example')` so that subdomains also work
options.why: Substring checks pass for `https://pay.example.evil.com` and similar names.

options.text: Reply with `targetOrigin` set to `'*'`, so the reply reaches the iframe even after it redirects
options.why: A wildcard may deliver your reply, perhaps with secrets, to whatever page is loaded there.

options.text: Check that `event.isTrusted` is true, which proves the message came from the iframe
options.why: postMessage events are trusted no matter who sent them, so this proves nothing.

explanation: postMessage is deliberately cross-origin, so the receiver must authenticate the sender with an exact origin comparison (or an allowlist) and validate the payload. Senders should pass an explicit targetOrigin so data can't leak if the frame navigates elsewhere.

stem: A custom element `<my-card>` attaches an open shadow root containing a `<button>`. A listener on the document runs `console.log(e.target.tagName, e.composedPath()[0].tagName)`. What does it log when the user clicks the button?

options.text: `BUTTON BUTTON`, because events report their real target to every listener
options.why: Events leaving a shadow tree are retargeted to the host.

options.text: `MY-CARD BUTTON`
options.why: Outside the shadow tree, target is retargeted to the host, but the open root still exposes the full path.

options.text: `MY-CARD MY-CARD`, because composedPath() hides the shadow tree from listeners outside it
options.why: Open shadow roots appear in composedPath; only closed ones are hidden.

options.text: Nothing, because click events do not cross shadow boundaries
options.why: click is a composed event, so it crosses into the light DOM.

explanation: Retargeting keeps shadow internals encapsulated. Listeners outside the component see the host as `event.target`, while listeners inside see the real button. `composedPath()` lists every node the event passes; for a closed shadow root, nodes inside it are left out when called from outside. Custom events only cross the boundary if created with `composed: true`.
reference: DOM Standard: Event retargeting; MDN: Event.composedPath()

stem: A single-page app router calls `history.pushState({}, '', '/orders')` when a link is clicked, and it renders views only inside a `popstate` listener. Users report two bugs: clicking links changes the URL but not the view, and refreshing on `/orders` gives a 404. Which two statements explain these bugs? (Choose two.)

options.text: `pushState` never fires `popstate`, so the router must render right after calling it
options.why: popstate fires only on history traversal, such as Back and Forward.

options.text: On refresh the browser requests `/orders` from the server, which must fall back to serving the app shell
options.why: pushState only changes the address bar, so the server needs to answer for that path.

options.text: `pushState` fires `popstate` only once the current task ends, so the render is just delayed
options.why: pushState never fires popstate, delayed or not.

options.text: `pushState` fires `hashchange` rather than `popstate`, so the router listens for the wrong event
options.why: hashchange only fires when the URL fragment changes during a navigation or traversal.

options.text: The Back button reloads the whole page from the server, so popstate can never fire in an SPA
options.why: Back between same-document history entries fires popstate without a reload.

explanation: A history-based router needs three pieces: intercept link clicks, call pushState and render, and render again on popstate (Back and Forward). The server or CDN must also rewrite unknown paths to index.html. The newer Navigation API (`navigation.addEventListener('navigate', …)`) unifies these cases where it is supported.
reference: MDN: History API; Window popstate event

stem: You deploy a new service worker. In a user's only open tab, the new worker installs and enters the `waiting` state. The user presses Reload. Which version controls the reloaded page?

options.text: The new worker, because reloading unloads the old page and frees the old worker
options.why: During a reload the old page is still a client when the new request starts.

options.text: The old worker; the new one waits until no tab uses the old one, unless it calls `skipWaiting()`
options.why: Reload overlaps the old and new pages, so the old worker is never released.

options.text: Neither: the page loads from the network with no service worker until the next visit
options.why: The active (old) worker keeps handling navigations.

options.text: The new worker, because a waiting worker takes over any navigation that is a reload
options.why: Waiting workers don't take control of reloads.

explanation: A new worker activates only when no clients use the old one. During a reload the current page isn't unloaded until the new response starts, so the old worker stays in charge. Fixes: close every tab, call `self.skipWaiting()` (optionally with `clients.claim()`), or show an 'Update available' prompt that triggers skipWaiting. The waiting step exists so one page never runs two versions.

stem: A page has the CSP `script-src 'self'` with no `'unsafe-inline'`. User files are served from the same origin under `/uploads/`, and an attacker can upload a `.js` file there. A bug lets them inject an arbitrary string through `container.innerHTML = userInput`. Which payload runs the attacker's script?

options.text: `<script src="/uploads/evil.js"></script>`, because it is same-origin and allowed by the policy
options.why: Script elements inserted with innerHTML are never executed, whatever their source.

options.text: ``, using the error handler to load the file
options.why: Inline event handlers count as inline script, which the policy blocks.

options.text: `<iframe srcdoc="<script src='/uploads/evil.js'></script>">`
options.why: The srcdoc document is parsed normally, inherits the origin and policy, and same-origin scripts pass.

options.text: None of them, because a script-src policy stops everything that innerHTML inserts
options.why: CSP limits where scripts come from; it can't tell an attacker's same-origin file from yours.

explanation: innerHTML doesn't run `<script>` elements, and the CSP blocks inline handlers. A srcdoc iframe is a new document built by the HTML parser, so its scripts execute. It inherits the parent's origin and CSP, and 'self' allows `/uploads/evil.js`. Same-origin user uploads and JSONP endpoints are well-known 'self' bypasses. Serve uploads from a separate sandbox domain, and prefer nonce- or hash-based strict CSPs.
reference: web.dev: Mitigate XSS with a strict CSP

options.text: `mo 1`, `mo 1`, `sync`, `p`, because each append notifies the observer immediately
options.why: Mutation observer callbacks never run synchronously.

options.text: `sync`, `p`, `mo 2`, because the observer runs as a task after all microtasks
options.why: Observer callbacks run in a microtask, not a later task.

options.text: `sync`, `mo 2`, `p`
options.why: The first mutation queues the observer microtask before the promise callback is queued, and both records are batched.

options.text: `sync`, `mo 1`, `mo 1`, `p`, because the observer runs once per record
options.why: Records are batched into one callback call.

explanation: The first mutation queues a 'notify mutation observers' microtask, and later mutations just add records to the same batch. After the script, the microtask queue runs in FIFO order: first the observer (with 2 records), then the promise reaction queued later. This batching is why MutationObserver is cheap compared with the old synchronous mutation events.

stem: An app stores the user's access token in `localStorage` and reads it on every API call. Which three statements are accurate concerns? (Choose three.)

options.text: Any script running on the origin, including injected XSS, can read the token
options.why: localStorage has no equivalent of HttpOnly.

options.text: Every read and write is synchronous and can block the main thread
options.why: The Web Storage API is synchronous and may hit disk.

options.text: It stores only strings, so objects must be serialised and parsed
options.why: Values are converted to strings, so objects need JSON.stringify and JSON.parse.

options.text: The token is sent to the server automatically with every request, like a cookie
options.why: Web Storage is never attached to requests; your code must add it.

options.text: Service workers can read it directly, so the token leaks into them
options.why: Service workers have no access to localStorage.

explanation: localStorage is convenient but readable by any script on the origin, so an XSS bug becomes token theft. Common alternatives: an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite session cookie (then defend CSRF), or keep a short-lived access token in memory with refresh through an HttpOnly cookie. Use IndexedDB if you need asynchronous storage.
reference: OWASP: HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet (Local Storage)

stem: An analytics library sends a final "session ended" event with `fetch('/collect', { method: 'POST', body })` inside a `beforeunload` listener. On mobile, many of these events never arrive. What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Make the request synchronous with XMLHttpRequest so the page waits for it to finish
options.why: Browsers now ignore or block synchronous XHR during unload, and it hurts navigation.

options.text: Move the code into an `unload` listener, which fires more reliably than beforeunload
options.why: unload is even less reliable on mobile and also stops pages entering the back/forward cache.

options.text: Send on `visibilitychange` when the page is hidden, using `navigator.sendBeacon()` or `fetch` with `keepalive: true`
options.why: Hidden is the last reliably reported state, and both APIs outlive the page.

options.text: Wrap the fetch call in setTimeout so it runs after the page finishes unloading
options.why: Timers do not run once the page has been discarded.

explanation: Mobile browsers often kill or freeze pages without firing beforeunload or unload, and unload listeners stop the page entering the bfcache. The recommended pattern is to flush on `visibilitychange` with `document.visibilityState === 'hidden'`, using sendBeacon or keepalive fetch. Those requests keep going after the page is gone (keepalive bodies are limited to 64 KB).

stem: Which cookie name prefix makes the browser reject the cookie unless it is set with `Secure`, has `Path=/`, and has no `Domain` attribute (so it is locked to the exact host)? Type the prefix.
explanation: A cookie named `__Host-sid` can only be set over HTTPS, for path /, and without Domain, so a compromised or attacker-controlled sibling subdomain can't overwrite it (cookie tossing). The weaker `__Secure-` prefix only requires the Secure flag.

stem: A form highlights the active field with `form.addEventListener('focus', (e) => e.target.classList.add('active'))`. The listener never runs when users tab into the inputs. Which two changes make it work? (Choose two.)

options.text: Listen for `focusin` instead, which bubbles up from the inputs
options.why: focusin is the bubbling counterpart of focus.

options.text: Keep `focus` but register it in the capture phase: `form.addEventListener('focus', h, true)`
options.why: Capture-phase listeners on ancestors see events that don't bubble.

options.text: Add `{ passive: true }` so the browser delivers the focus events sooner
options.why: passive only concerns cancelling the event; it doesn't change propagation.

options.text: Set `form.onfocus = h` instead of using addEventListener
options.why: Handler properties use the same bubble phase, so they still miss focus from the inputs.

options.text: Give the form `tabindex="0"` so it receives focus events from its fields
options.why: That makes the form focusable itself; it doesn't make field focus events bubble.

explanation: Non-bubbling events still go through the capture phase, so an ancestor can catch them with a capture listener. Alternatively, use the bubbling equivalents (focusin/focusout). React's onFocus works because React listens for focusin under the hood.

stem: During one frame, code has scheduled a `requestAnimationFrame` callback that changes an element's width. Put the browser's work for that frame in order.

options.text: Run requestAnimationFrame callbacks
options.why: Scripts adjust the DOM for the frame first.

options.text: Recalculate styles
options.why: Computed styles are updated.

options.text: Layout
options.why: Geometry is calculated from the new styles.

options.text: Paint
options.why: Layers are drawn.

options.text: Composite
options.why: Layers are assembled into the frame.

explanation: rAF callbacks run just before the browser's rendering steps, so DOM changes made there are included in the same frame. Next come style, layout and paint, and the compositor assembles the layers. Reading layout inside rAF after writes still forces an early layout, so keep reads before writes there too.
